chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
title: The Silver Slipper on Chicago's South Side
summary: The band opens at a big Chinese restaurant-club; the owner puts up Davison and his wife in an incense-filled flat; musicians' good times in Prohibition.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: All right so you went back to Chicago --
Well, we went back and, uh, yes -- I was married -- to Smiley - because when we went back to
Chicago, we went on the South side of Chicago and I played the Crystal-- the Silver Slipper --
The Silver Slipper-- the place owned by that Chinese man---
It was a Chinese restaurant--- it was a fantastic one -- great hugh one. I remember it had palm trees all around the floor--

Well, I guess - I should get around to that--- but, anyway, we opened there and it was a marvelous job and, uh, of course, then I surely thought in my mind I could get my wife back - she knew I was doing so good. And, so, I told the boss - the Chinese guy - that--- about my wife. And, he said -- well, I've got a flat -- he said, I keep a woman and he said, she has plenty of room and you and your wife can move in there for the time being anyway -- it won't cost you much. And, I thought that was a marvelous idea. So, my wife did show up and we moved in there; I'll never forget when I walked in that apartment, it looked like a Chinese temple-- it had beads hanging on the doors and all kinds of screwy lamps and, uh, those things that you burn incense all around the place. Well, anyway, that's another story. But, the point is that we stayed there a long time and he liked us. And, it was-- if you really want to know how things were in those days -- it was a fun time in life for musicians. There were so many jobs and there was so many people that liked it and there was so much boot-leg whiskey around

and everybody seemed to - at that point - I think, if you tell somebody, you're not allowed to drink -- that's when they're going to drink the most and I think, in those days, even the women were getting drunk, which - you know - and all this---
And, there were hundreds of bands in Chicago - weren't there?
